common_name: Plum Farmer Black Raspberry (Early-Season Ohio Heirloom Black Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tip layers in early spring into well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, spacing plants to allow good air circulation around the vigorous summer growth.

directions: Plum Farmer is an old black raspberry selection that traces to Ohio in the early twentieth century and remained a mainstay of home and market gardens for decades because of its heavy early crop. Canes are notably vigorous and arch widely, so tip-prune new growth in summer to encourage branching and keep the planting manageable. Fruit ripens earlier than most other black raspberry selections, giving a jump on the harvest season ahead of later cultivars. Renew the planting by rooting cane tips that touch the ground, since black raspberries spread this way rather than by root suckers.
sources: Ohio State University Extension — Black Raspberry Production
USDA Agricultural Research Service — black raspberry germplasm studies

common_name: New Logan Black Raspberry (Pacific Northwest Processing Black Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this self-fertile selection needs no second variety nearby to set a full crop.

directions: New Logan is a vigorous, self-fertile black raspberry grown widely in Oregon and Washington for both fresh market and processing, where its firm, flavorful berries hold up well to machine harvest. Upright, thorny canes produce a dependable midsummer crop and benefit from summer tipping to encourage lateral branching, which increases next year's fruiting wood. It performs well in the cool, wet-winter/dry-summer climate of the Pacific Northwest but adapts to other temperate regions with similar chill accumulation. Cut fruited canes to the ground after harvest to make room for the current season's new growth.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Raspberry Cultivars for the Pacific Northwest

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, following the same tip-layering and summer-pruning regimen used for other black raspberry cultivars.

directions: Hanover is a black raspberry cultivar grown commercially in Pacific Northwest trial plantings and has been included in research comparing fruit color and antioxidant content across black raspberry selections. Like other black raspberries, it forms an upright, arching, thorny cane that fruits on second-year wood, so first-year canes should be tipped in summer to promote branching rather than allowed to grow unchecked. Harvest the small, dark, dome-shaped berries by hand in midsummer as they separate cleanly from the receptacle. Remove spent fruiting canes at ground level after harvest to reduce disease carryover and make room for new primocanes.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — anthocyanin and phenolic variation studies in black raspberry cultivars

common_name: John Robertson Black Raspberry (Heirloom Jelly Black Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tip layers in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun, giving plants room to arch and spread during the growing season.

directions: John Robertson is an older heirloom black raspberry long valued among home growers for fruit that is especially well suited to jelly and preserves, thanks to good natural pectin and a rich, concentrated flavor when cooked down. It shares the typical black raspberry growth habit of upright, arching, thorny canes that fruit on the previous year's wood, so tip new canes in summer to encourage branching and a fuller crop the following year. Propagate by rooting the arching cane tips where they touch soil in late summer, then sever and transplant the rooted tip the following spring. Remove old fruited canes after harvest to keep the planting open and reduce disease pressure.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — black raspberry germplasm diversity studies
